summary: Surveys use of IPv4 addresses in IETF Sub-IP Area standards-track and experimental documents, to find dependencies on IPv4. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A checklist of rules for the lowest layers that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in sub-ip area specs
subtitle: A catalog of IPv4 address dependencies in Sub-IP area standards.

tldr.problem: As the internet transitions from IPv4 to IPv6, standards that assume IPv4 addressing could become obstacles.
tldr.mechanism: This document surveys all standards-track and experimental RFCs in the IETF Sub-IP Area to identify IPv4 dependencies. The Sub-IP Area covers technologies like MPLS, label switching, and link-layer protocols.
tldr.outcome: The survey found zero IPv4 dependencies among the 7 RFCs in scope. Most Sub-IP technologies are addressing-independent or already support both IPv4 and IPv6.

today: RFC 3793 is Informational and documents the Sub-IP Area's IPv6 readiness as of May 2004. The findings remain valid—MPLS and label-switching technologies have no inherent IPv4 dependencies and continue to work with both address families. This document provides lasting assurance that Sub-IP standards support IPv6 transition without requiring updates.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This survey document is part of a series examining IPv6 readiness across IETF areas. This RFC focuses on the Sub-IP Area, which manages technologies that operate below the IP layer or work with IP independent of version, such as Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), label distribution protocols, and link-layer technologies.

By design, Sub-IP technologies operate at a level of abstraction that often makes them address-family independent. However, some protocols might carry IPv4 addresses in payloads or examples, so this survey examines whether any contain IPv4-specific requirements.
sections.eli5: This document checks the lowest levels of network plumbing to see if any of them require old-style addresses.

sections.title: Scope and Coverage
sections.content:
The Sub-IP Area survey examined 7 RFCs total: 0 Full Standards, 0 Draft Standards, 6 Proposed Standards, and 1 Experimental RFC. The scope is narrower than other area surveys because Sub-IP is a smaller area with fewer published standards. The RFCs examined include MPLS architecture and protocols, label switching over various media (Frame Relay, ATM), and the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP).

Each RFC was examined to determine whether its core protocol or procedures depend on IPv4-specific features, even if examples or implementations might use IPv4 addresses.
sections.eli5: The document checks 7 network standards. They're mostly about routing labels and protocols that work with any address style.

sections.title: Zero IPv4 Dependencies Found
sections.content:
The survey found zero RFCs with IPv4 dependencies in the Sub-IP Area. None of the 6 Proposed Standards or 1 Experimental RFC contain provisions that require IPv4 or assume IPv4 addressing. This reflects the inherent design of label-switching technologies: they operate independently of the addressing scheme used in the IP layer.

The MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) and the Label Stack Encoding (RFC 3032) are explicitly address-independent. The Label Distribution Protocol (RFC 3036) is described as both IPv4 and IPv6 aware and requires no changes. Link-layer label switching technologies also have no IPv4-specific requirements.
sections.eli5: None of the network standards checked need old-style addresses. They all work with any kind of address system.

sections.title: Implications for IPv6 Transition
sections.content:
The lack of IPv4 dependencies in Sub-IP standards means this area poses no barriers to IPv6 transition. MPLS and label-switching technologies will function identically whether carrying IPv4 or IPv6 traffic. This is a significant advantage because Sub-IP technologies are fundamental to internet backbone and carrier operations.

Organizations deploying IPv6 need not be concerned about Sub-IP standards blocking the transition. The standards can carry both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic without modification, making Sub-IP a stable foundation for dual-stack and eventual IPv6-only deployments.
sections.eli5: The lowest level of the network doesn't care which address type flows through it. This makes switching to the new addresses much easier.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 3793 is an Informational document that confirmed the Sub-IP Area was well-designed for version independence. The survey remains valid as evidence that label-switching and Sub-IP technologies do not impede IPv6 transition.

For network operators and service providers, this document provides assurance that upgrading infrastructure to dual-stack or IPv6-only does not require standards updates at the Sub-IP layer. The technologies are ready to support both address families without modification.
sections.eli5: This document proves that the network's lowest layers are ready for new addresses with no changes needed.
